# Model Description Summary

A concise guide to choosing from the available AI models for C# software development, refactoring, technical documentation, experimentation, and repository maintenance.

## Recommended models by task

| Task | First models to try |
|---|---|
| Complex implementation, debugging, and multi-file changes | **GPT-5.3-Codex** or **Claude Opus 5.5** |
| Everyday C# development and refactoring | **Claude Sonnet 5.5** or **GPT-6 Sol** |
| Architecture and high-risk code review | **Claude Opus 5.5** |
| XML documentation, manuals, and explanations | **Claude Sonnet 5.5** or **GPT-6 Luna** |
| Repository cleanup and maintainability | **GPT-5.3-Codex** or **Claude Sonnet 5.5** |
| Quick, simple questions and edits | **GPT-5.4 nano 1**, **Gemini 3.8 Flash**, or **Claude Haiku 5.5** |
| Vibe-coding and open-ended exploration | **GPT-6 Astra**, **Claude Opus 5.5**, or **Grok 4.7** |
| Independent second opinion | **Kimi K3** or **Gemini 4 Argon** |

These are starting points, not guarantees. For consequential code changes, ask a capable model to explain assumptions, identify affected files, propose tests, and review its own diff. Compile and test the result locally.

## Practical workflow

| Stage | Recommended approach |
|---|---|
| **Implement** | Start with GPT-5.3-Codex or Claude Sonnet 5.5. Escalate especially difficult problems to Claude Opus 5.5. |
| **Refactor and review** | Ask for code smells, duplication, coupling, compatibility concerns, and missing tests. Use a second model for an independent review of significant changes. |
| **Document** | Start with Claude Sonnet 5.5 or a GPT-6 variant that performs well in your own tests. Supply the audience, project conventions, and existing examples. |
| **Maintain repositories** | Have a coding-oriented model inspect structure, naming, project boundaries, build configuration, and obsolete files. Request a plan before broad changes. |
| **Experiment** | Keep vibe-coded prototypes isolated. Review dependencies, security, licensing, and maintainability before merging them. |

## Important .NET guidance

Always specify whether the target is **.NET 10** or **.NET Framework 4.8**. Their APIs, runtime behavior, tooling, and library compatibility differ. Explicitly instruct the model not to use APIs unavailable on the target framework and to state compatibility assumptions.

For repository changes, ask the model to inspect existing patterns, keep changes focused, preserve public APIs unless asked otherwise, add or update tests, run or specify build/test commands, and summarize changed files and unverified risks.

## Choosing between models

The model names—especially provider-specific variants such as Astra, Luna, Sol, Terra, Fable, and Argon—do not always reveal their exact technical capabilities. Treat recommendations as starting points, not guaranteed rankings.

Compare candidate models using the same real tasks from your codebase:

| Evaluation area | What to check |
|---|---|
| **Correctness** | Does the code compile and meet the requirements? |
| **Framework awareness** | Does it respect the .NET target? |
| **Repository awareness** | Does it follow existing architecture and conventions? |
| **Refactoring quality** | Does it improve maintainability without needless abstractions? |
| **Documentation quality** | Is it accurate and consistent with the code? |
| **Tool reliability** | Does it correctly inspect and modify files? |
| **Efficiency** | Is the quality worth the latency or cost? |

Reassess your preferred models as providers update them and as your own evaluation results change.
